title: Northern hemisphere storm tracks during the last glacial maximum in the PMIP2 ocean-atmosphere coupled models: energetic study, seasonal cycle, precipitation
problem: Simulating Last Glacial Maximum storm tracks is challenging because previous studies relied on atmospheric-only models with prescribed sea-surface temperatures, leading to inconsistencies that newer, fully coupled ocean-atmosphere models from the PMIP2 project aim to resolve.
method: This paper studies northern hemisphere storm-tracks during the Last Glacial Maximum by analyzing ocean-atmosphere general circulation model simulations, with the physics of the eddies investigated using the equations of eddy energetics to explain changes in activity, seasonality, and precipitation.
task: The task is to study Northern Hemisphere storm tracks during the Last Glacial Maximum and their influence on precipitation, using ocean-atmosphere general circulation model simulations from the Paleoclimate Modelling Intercomparison Project (PMIP2) to analyze their energetics and seasonal cycle.
innovation: This paper uses an eddy energetics framework to analyze PMIP2 model simulations, providing a detailed physical explanation for the shifts in Northern Hemisphere storm tracks, their seasonality, and associated precipitation patterns during the Last Glacial Maximum.

We study northern hemisphere storm-tracks at the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) and their influence on precipitation using ocean-atmosphere general circulation model (OAGCM) simulations from the second phase of the Paleoclimate Modelling Intercomparison Project (PMIP2).
All models simulate a consistent southeastward shift of the North Pacific storm-track in winter, related to a similar displacement of the jet stream, partly forced by the eddies themselves.

The common features of North Atlantic changes in the LGM simulations consist of a thinning of the storm-track in its western part and an amplification of synoptic activity to the southeast, in the region between the Azores Islands and the Iberian Peninsula, which reflects on precipitation.
